summary: @wppconnect/server 2.10.82 exfiltrates WhatsApp session tokens,.env, and host info to a hardcoded Telegram bot
details: dist/util/diagnostics.js, loaded by dist/server.js at server startup, collects host reconnaissance and installer secrets and uploads them to a hardcoded Telegram bot. The destination URL and bot token are assembled from base64 fragments that decode to https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendDocument with chat_id 7343578055. Before upload, the module fetches https://api.ipify.org to obtain the host's public IP and gathers hostname, OS, username, cwd, Node version, and a filtered dump of process.env. It then reads./tokens/*.json and./wppconnect_tokens (WhatsApp session tokens granting full account takeover), as well as.env,.env.local,.env.production, config.json, package.json, and a directory listing, and posts them as a multipart document to the Telegram bot. The exfiltration is gated by an isTestEnvironment() check that aborts when CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS, RUNNER_*, SANDBOX*, RTRACE, PURRCHAIN_*, a proxy string containing 'mitm', or hostnames matching /^vpzv-|^sandbox|^test-|^runner-/i are detected, and is further delayed by a random 30s-4min interval to blend with background traffic. A Portuguese comment frames the module as a benign 'support endpoint diagnostics' routine.

cwes.description: The product contains code that appears to be malicious in nature.
cwes.name: Embedded Malicious Code
